core_message: A Russian family lived completely cut off in the Siberian taiga for over 40 years and never heard of the Second World War.
title: The Family That Missed World War Two
description:
In 1978, a helicopter carrying Soviet geologists over the remote Abakan region of the Siberian taiga spotted a cleared, cultivated patch more than 200 km from the nearest settlement. It belonged to the Lykovs, a family of Old Believers. In 1936, after his brother was shot by a Communist patrol, Karp Lykov fled into the forest with his wife Akulina and their children Savin and Natalia; Dmitry and Agafia were born in the wilderness. They lived for more than 40 years with almost no outside contact, mainly on potatoes; in 1961 Akulina died of starvation after a hard frost destroyed their crops. When the geologists arrived, the family knew nothing of the Second World War. In 1981, Savin, Natalia and Dmitry died within months of each other; Karp died in 1988. Agafia, the youngest, chose to stay in the taiga.

Sources: Wikipedia, Lykov family; Smithsonian Magazine, For 40 Years, This Russian Family Was Cut Off From All Human Contact.

scenes.narration: In 1978, a Soviet helicopter flying over the Siberian wilderness spotted something impossible: a garden, more than two hundred kilometres from the nearest village.
Back in 1936, Karp Lykov had fled into the forest with his wife and two children, escaping religious persecution.
They lived alone for over forty years. Two more children were born out there. They survived mostly on potatoes, and after one hard frost, the mother starved to death.
When the geologists finally walked up to their hut, the Lykovs had never heard of the Second World War.
In 1981, three of the children died within months, and Karp died in 1988. His youngest daughter, Agafia, chose to stay on in the taiga.
